summary: Defines terms used when benchmarking ATM based switching devices, so test results can be described and compared consistently. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Before racing, everyone agrees on what words like lap and finish mean. This does that for testing network switches.

subtitle: Defines terms and metrics for testing and comparing ATM network switches.

tldr.problem: ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) switches are complex devices with many performance characteristics. Without agreed-upon terminology, test results cannot be compared or reproduced fairly across different products and test labs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a comprehensive set of formal definitions and performance metrics organized around the B-ISDN reference model, which divides ATM functionality into four layers (services, AAL, ATM, physical) and two planes (user and control). Each definition explains what the term means and how it affects IP and TCP performance.
tldr.outcome: Network engineers and researchers can now describe and compare ATM switch benchmarks consistently, understanding trade-offs like how different traffic service categories (CBR, VBR, UBR) balance throughput, delay, and loss guarantees.

today: RFC 2761 is an Informational document describing benchmarking terminology for ATM devices. While ATM technology usage has declined with the rise of Ethernet and IP-based networking, this RFC remains relevant for organizations that still operate or test ATM infrastructure.

sections.title: Why ATM Needs Benchmarking Terms
sections.content:
ATM, or Asynchronous Transfer Mode, is a network technology that breaks data into small fixed-size units called cells (53 octets each). Because ATM devices have many configuration options and performance characteristics, there was no standard way to compare them. This RFC extends the benchmarking terminology already established for general network devices in RFC 1242 and RFC 2544, specializing it for ATM switches.

The challenge is that ATM has multiple layers and service categories, each with different impacts on real application performance. The RFC provides terms that let testers measure what matters: how well ATM carries IP data, how TCP throughput is affected, and what happens under congestion or error conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM is a complicated way to move data around networks. Testing it requires special names for all its features so everyone knows what they are testing.

sections.title: The B-ISDN Reference Model
sections.content:
The RFC uses the B-ISDN (Broadband ISDN) reference model as its organizational framework. This model divides ATM functionality into four horizontal layers and two vertical planes.

The four layers, from top to bottom, are: Services (where IP runs), AAL (Adaptation Layer, which converts higher-layer data into ATM cells), ATM (the core cell switching and forwarding), and Physical (the actual cables and media). The two planes are the User Plane (carrying actual data like IP packets) and the Control Plane (handling signaling and management).

This structure matters because performance issues in one layer affect everything above it. For example, if the AAL layer takes too long to convert a large IP packet into many ATM cells, it can delay TCP retransmission timing and reduce throughput.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM has layers like a sandwich: IP data on top, cells at the bottom, and adapters and switches in between. This RFC explains how to test each layer and how problems in one layer hurt the layers above.

sections.title: Traffic Service Categories
sections.content:
The RFC defines three main ATM service categories that determine how the network treats a connection, each with different trade-offs for bandwidth, delay, and loss.

Constant Bit Rate (CBR) is like a reserved telephone call: it guarantees a fixed bandwidth and minimal delay variation, making it ideal for voice or video. However, even if a CBR connection is idle, it reserves its bandwidth and cannot share it with other connections.

Variable Bit Rate (VBR) is for applications that need good throughput but can tolerate some variation. It specifies both a peak rate (the most cells per second that will be sent) and a sustainable average rate. VBR can be more efficient than CBR when applications have bursty traffic patterns.

Unspecified Bit Rate (UBR) is the best-effort service, similar to regular IP. There are no guarantees about bandwidth, delay, or whether cells will be delivered. UBR is cheap but risky for applications sensitive to loss or delay.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM offers three speed classes: reserved (CBR, like a direct phone line), medium (VBR, like a highway that gets busier), and best-effort (UBR, like shipping packages with no guarantee).

sections.title: Performance Metrics and Impairments
sections.content:
The RFC defines many metrics that affect how well ATM carries IP traffic. Key impairments include Cell Loss (cells that are dropped during transmission), Cell Delay Variation (when cells arrive at irregular intervals), Cell Misinsertion (a cell sent to the wrong destination), and Cell Errors (corruption detected by the header check).

Each of these has a cascading effect on the AAL layer's Segmentation and Reassembly (SAR) process. When a cell is lost, the entire IP packet it belonged to is usually discarded because AAL5 (the dominant adaptation layer) can detect the missing cell through a length check but cannot recover it. This makes even a small cell loss ratio significantly impact TCP throughput.

The RFC also defines traffic control parameters like Peak Cell Rate (PCR), Sustainable Cell Rate (SCR), and Burst Tolerance (BT), which together define how much traffic a connection can send and how long it can burst above its average rate.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM can have problems like lost cells, cells arriving late, or cells going to the wrong place. Each problem breaks IP packets in different ways, hurting Internet performance.

sections.title: Permanent and Switched Connections
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes between Permanent Virtual Circuits (PVCs), which are set up once and left up indefinitely, and Switched Virtual Circuits (SVCs), which are established on-demand through signaling.

For SVCs, the signaling process can take significant time (up to 20 seconds in worst case), which affects the initial TCP round-trip time measurement and overall throughput. This matters because TCP's congestion control algorithm relies on accurate round-trip time estimates.

The RFC also covers both Virtual Channels (VCs) and Virtual Paths (VPs). A Virtual Path is a bundle of Virtual Channels, allowing the network to treat groups of connections as a unit for routing and management.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM connections can be permanent (like a dedicated line) or set up on demand (like making a phone call). Setting up a new call can take time, which slows down Internet applications at the start.
